title: Print every door's tag at once
allegory: A Q-network is like a tag printer you carry from room to room: show it a snapshot of any room, even one nobody has seen, and it prints a price tag for every exit at once, so you never need a book listing every room in the world.
map: a snapshot of the room: a few measurements
the observation vector s (four numbers in CartPole)
the printer's gears, tuned by experience
the MLP's weights θ, trained towards TD targets
one tag per exit, printed in one go
an output layer with one unit per action: Q_θ(s) ∈ ℝ^|A|
walking through the exit with the biggest tag
the greedy action argmax_a Q_θ(s, a)
a room nobody has seen still gets sensible tags
generalisation: similar states share weights, so unvisited states get values
credit: Framing borrowed from Andrew Ng, Machine Learning Specialization (reinforcement learning, 'Improved neural network architecture'): one network outputs every action's Q-value at once.

cap.1: A book of scores needs a page for every situation. But a balancing pole can lean by any amount, so the pages never end and most situations have none.
cap.2: Tabular Q-learning keeps one entry per (state, action). CartPole's observation is four continuous numbers, so states almost never repeat exactly, and an unvisited entry keeps its starting value.
cap.3: A lookup table cannot generalise: Q(s, a) changes only when (s, a) itself is updated. With continuous observations you need a parametric Q_θ that shares statistical strength across nearby states.

cap.1: So swap the book for a printer. Show it a snapshot of the room and out come price tags for every exit at once. Brand-new rooms get tags too.
cap.2: The Q-network is that printer: a small MLP that takes the observation and returns a vector with one Q-value per action. Unseen states still get values, because similar inputs give similar outputs.
cap.3: Q_θ: S → ℝ^|A| replaces the table with a function approximator. It generalises across states through shared weights θ, and its outputs are only as good as the TD targets it was fitted to.

cap.1: The printer's rule: snapshot in, a short list of scores out, one per exit. To choose, read the list once and take the biggest.
cap.2: Input size is the observation size; output size is the number of actions. The QNetwork exercise builds this MLP. Picking the greedy action is argmax over one forward pass, not one pass per action.
cap.3: Emitting all |A| values at once makes both the greedy argmax and max_a Q(s′, a) in the TD target a single forward pass. It also presumes a finite, discrete action set.

chapters.name: Nudge one, move many

left.title: Q-table
lines: unseen rows stay at the start value

chapters.verdict: Sharing is the power, and also why the target keeps moving.

cap.1: Retune the printer for one room and the tags for similar rooms change too. That's how new rooms get sensible tags, and also how old tags drift.
cap.2: A gradient step on one transition moves shared weights, so Q shifts for nearby states, including s′. The target you just aimed at has moved: this is why DQN adds a target network.
cap.3: Function approximation couples updates across states. With bootstrapping and off-policy data it forms the deadly triad, with no convergence guarantee; replay and a target network are engineering patches.

chapters.name: Only the taken tag
chapters.title: a batch of 4 memories: only the lit cells learn

cap.1: Each memory only says what happened after one exit, so only that exit's tag gets corrected. The other tags on that snapshot are left alone.
cap.2: The network outputs every action, but a transition (s, a, r, s′) only tells you about a. Gather Q_θ(s)[a] for the taken action and regress that entry. Some rows are exploration moves, and that's fine.
cap.3: Loss per sample: (Q_θ(s)[a] − y)² with y = r + γ·max_a′ Q_θ⁻(s′, a′)·(1 − terminated). Only the taken action's output gets gradient; the max belongs on the target side, at s′.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: State in, every action's score out
Finite actions only: max needs a list
Read the scores to see what it wants

cap.1: A printer that scores every option at a glance lets an agent act in worlds too big for any book. Read its tags and you see what it wants before it moves.
cap.2: Swapping the table for a Q-network turned Q-learning into DQN, which learned 49 Atari games from pixels. Its per-action outputs are also an inspection point: log them to see what the agent values.
cap.3: In DQN, Q_θ is the whole policy: act greedily on its outputs. Understanding or steering such an agent starts with what those outputs encode. Continuous actions break the max, which is why policy gradients come next.

coda.title: Slide the pole's lean: the network tags every state, the table knows three
coda.f: (() => { const k = 3*(lean + 0.5*spin); const seen = [-0.5, 0, 0.5].some(v => abs(lean - v) < 0.001) && abs(spin) < 0.001; return [5 - k, 5 + k, seen ? 5 - k : 0, seen ? 5 + k : 0]; })()

readouts.label: network's pick
readouts.f: (() => { const k = 3*(lean + 0.5*spin); return abs(k) < 1e-9 ? 'tie: either push' : (k > 0 ? 'push right' : 'push left'); })()

readouts.label: table's pick
readouts.f: (() => { const k = 3*(lean + 0.5*spin); const seen = [-0.5, 0, 0.5].some(v => abs(lean - v) < 0.001) && abs(spin) < 0.001; return !seen ? 'no row for this state: tags still 0' : (abs(k) < 1e-9 ? 'tie: either push' : (k > 0 ? 'push right' : 'push left')); })()

readouts.label: lean where the network's pick flips

caption.1: Slide the lean. The network's tags change smoothly everywhere. The table has rows for just three exact states: step off them and its tags go blank.
caption.2: This toy network prefers push right when lean plus half the swing is positive: move the cart under the falling pole. The table can only answer for exact states it has stored.
caption.3: Toy Q_θ, linear in (lean, swing); the tabular Q holds entries only at visited states, initialised to 0. Generalisation is what lets DQN act in continuous state spaces, and why its targets move.

where_else: A language model's unembedding: one logit per vocabulary token from a single pass
Image classifiers: one output per class, then argmax to decide
Actor-critic methods: a critic network estimates value where a table could not
Any learned scorer that rates a fixed menu of options in one go

hamming.what: A neural network that takes a state and returns one Q-value per action, replacing the Q-table.
hamming.when: Whenever states are too many or too continuous to list, but the actions are a small finite menu, as in CartPole or Atari.
hamming.why: A table can only answer for states it has visited; a network shares what it learned across similar states, and one forward pass scores every action.

object.title: The tag landscape
object.subtitle: every state on the floor, each action's tag as height
object.f: (() => { const hill = 10 - 3*(x*x + y*y); const L = hill - 2*(x + 0.5*y); const R = hill + 2*(x + 0.5*y); return m == 0 ? L : (m == 1 ? R : max(L, R)); })()

knobs.label: which tag: 0 push left, 1 push right, 2 the bigger one

cap.1: Every spot on the floor is a state: how far the pole leans, how fast it swings. Height is the 'push left' tag. Upright and still is the high ground.
cap.2: This sheet is Q_θ(s, left) over a 2D slice of state space, lean by swing. A toy, shaped like CartPole: near upright either push keeps the pole up for a long while.
cap.3: Q_θ(·, left) evaluated on a grid of states. A table stores values only at visited points; the network defines a whole function, fitted where data exists and interpolated elsewhere.

cap.1: Now the 'push right' tag: the same hill, tilted the other way. Pushing right pays when the pole leans or swings right.
cap.2: Same network, second output unit. Both sheets come out of one forward pass; they differ only in the last layer's weights for each action.
cap.3: The two action values share every hidden layer and differ only in the final linear readout, so features learned for one action serve the other.

cap.1: Keep only the bigger tag at each spot. A crease appears: on one side the printer says left, on the other it says right.
cap.2: max_a Q_θ(s, a) is the upper envelope of the two sheets. The crease is the decision boundary, where both tags tie: here, the line lean + swing/2 = 0.
cap.3: The greedy value is the pointwise max of the action values; argmax flips across the tie set. Near that crease, small estimation errors flip the chosen action.

cap.1: The three pins mark the only rooms a table had pages for. The printer covers the whole floor, including every gap between the pins.
cap.2: A tabular Q would hold numbers at those pins and nothing in between. The network answers everywhere, which is the point and also the risk: in the gaps it is guessing.
cap.3: Generalisation away from the data is inductive bias, not knowledge. Where the replay buffer never went, Q_θ is extrapolating, and a greedy policy will trust it anyway.

predict.q: The pole leans right and is swinging further right. Which tag is bigger?
predict.why: Pushing the cart under the falling pole keeps it up. On this toy, push right wins wherever lean plus half the swing is positive.

predict.q: How many forward passes does it take to pick the greedy action for one state?
predict.why: The network prints every action's value at once, so the argmax needs a single pass.

predict.q: You train on a state with lean 0.30. What happens to the tags at lean 0.31?
predict.why: Shared weights move nearby states together. That is generalisation, and it is also why the TD target moves.

object.where: Any network with one output per option: a classifier's logits, a language model's next-token scores.
